sm: The episode, from Discovery Science and featuring Michael Behe, asks what information is, why life needs so much of it, and where it comes from. Information is described as a series of simple decisions, and DNA stores it as a sequence of four chemicals arranged like letters in a book. Genes hold the instructions for proteins, which are copied into messenger RNA by one machine and read by the ribosome, another machine, to build proteins. The narrator says human DNA carries instructions for more than twenty thousand proteins and about two hundred cell types. He points to protein machines like ATP synthase and kinesin, to cell-to-cell signaling, and to timing, such as genes for teeth switching on and off, with elephants getting six to seven sets. The roughly three billion base pairs would fill about a million pages in book form, and science still lacks a full description of the information needed to build even one cell.

The second part imagines writing a manual for building a human thigh bone, the femur. It would cover cartilage forming first, minerals hardening parts of it, attachment points for muscles and tendons, and growth plates that must each be told when and how much to grow so the bone stays in proportion with the muscles. Bone cells must stay active for life to repair fractures and thicken under heavy loads, and the marrow and blood vessels coordinate with the circulatory, immune, muscular and nervous systems. The narrator calls this a marvel of engineering that shows foresight and a prearranged plan. Turning to origins, he argues that orderly chemical shapes in nature are not working code, and that a gradual start for DNA hits a chicken and egg problem, since DNA needs proteins and proteins need DNA. He concludes that source code this sophisticated has never been known to arise without a programmer, so the designer and supplier of the information is an intelligent agent.
